ABSTRACT: The different enantiomers of specific chiral
molecules frequently exhibit disparate biological, physiological, or
pharmacological properties. Therefore, the efficient synthesis of
single enantiomers is of particular importance not only to the
pharmaceutical sector but also to other industrial sectors, such as
agrochemical and fine chemical industries. Deracemization, a
process during which a racemic mixture is converted into a
nonracemic product with 100% atom economy and theoretical
yield, is the most straightforward method to access enantioenriched molecules but a challenging task due to a decrease in entropy
and microscopic reversibility. Axially chiral allenes bear a distinctive structure of two orthogonal cumulative π-systems and are
acknowledged as synthetically versatile synthons in organic synthesis. The selective creation of axially chiral allenes with high optical
purity under mild reaction conditions has always been a very popular and hot topic in organic synthesis but remains challenging.
Herein, a photoexcited palladium-catalyzed deracemization of nonprefunctionalized disubstituted allenes is disclosed. This method
provides an efficient and economical strategy to accommodate a broad scope of allenes with good enantioselectivities and yields (53
examples, up to 96% yield and 95% ee). The use of a suitable chiral palladium complex with visible light irradiation is an essential
factor in achieving this transformation. A metal-to-ligand charge transfer mechanism was proposed based on control experiments and
density functional theory calculations. Quantum mechanical studies implicate dual modes of asymmetric induction behind our new
protocol: (1) sterically controlled stereoselective binding of one allene enantiomer under the ground-state and (2) facile,
noncovalent interaction-driven excited-state isomerization toward the opposite enantiomer. The success of this newly established
photochemical deracemization strategy should provide inspiration for expansion to other multisubstituted allenes and will open up a
new mode for enantioselective excited-state palladium catalysis.
■
INTRODUCTION
The different enantiomers of specific chiral molecules, such as
small-molecule drugs, frequently exhibit disparate biological,
physiological, or pharmacological properties.
1
It is not
surprising that one enantiomer of a chiral drug is clinically
effective and the other optical isomer can produce unwanted or
even catastrophic side effects.
2,3
Therefore, the efficient
synthesis of single enantiomers is of particular importance
not only to the pharmaceutical sector but also to other
industrial sectors, such as agrochemical and fine chemical
industries.
4
Mother Nature produces sugars and amino acids as
a single enantiomer in biological systems, which results in the
homochirality of living organisms.
5
Regrettably, the range of
chiral pools provided by nature is limited in terms of structure
and stereochemistry. Asymmetric synthesis has been evolved as
a powerful synthetic platform for the construction of diverse
enantioenriched molecules in the most efficient and practical
manner during the past few decades.
6,7
However, the
identification of a highly enantioselective chiral reagent
8
or
catalyst
9
for a certain reaction is not always an easy task. A
well-established alternative strategy relies on classic or kinetic
resolution process of a racemic mixture but with a maximum
50% theoretical yield of the desired product and the recovered
substrate.
10−12
Deracemization, as defined by Pirkle,
13
is a process “in which
a racemate is made nonracemic by increasing the quantity of
one enantiomer at the expense of the other”. The
deracemization process offers a 100% atom-economic protocol
without the release of any byproducts. However, since such a
process represents a reaction in the energetic uphill direction,
external energy is required to provide the entropy balance.
Moreover, the principle of microscopic reversibility makes this
process kinetically challenging (Figure 1a).
14
Visible (solar)
light, as a sustainable energy source, can supply the necessary
external perturbation to drive the deracemization reaction
forward. Therefore, photochemical deracemization mediated
by visible light has gained attention from the chemistry
community, and some breakthroughs have been achieved
recently.
15−32
Bach and co-workers reported visible-light-
driven deracemization of amide-containing allenes mediated
by the hydrogen bonding between chiral photosensitizer and

The different overall sensitization
rates of two enantiomers are responsible for this deracemiza-

18
and Bach
23
also demonstrated photo-
chemical deracemization of 5-substituted hydantoins and 4-
substituted imidazolidin-2-ones, respectively, through asym-
metric hydrogen atom transfer. Meggers/Chen
21
and Luo
24
achieved deracemization of α-branched ketones and aldehydes,
respectively, through photochemical asymmetric proton trans-
fer. These achievements showcase that the photochemical
processes are valuable synthetic means for the deracemization.
However, racemic substrates must be sophisticatedly designed
and prefunctionalized properly.
Axially chiral allenes are acknowledged as synthetically
versatile synthons in organic synthesis and bear a distinctive
structure of two orthogonal cumulative π-systems.
33−35
Moreover, chiral allenes are ubiquitous in advanced functional
materials
36
and naturally occurring products.
37,38
Undoubt-
edly, the exploration of high-efficiency approaches for
asymmetric synthesis of optically active allenes has received
considerable attention of chemists.
39−42
Although a series of
efficient approaches, involving allenyl cations,
43
allenyl
anions,
44−46
allenyl radicals,
47,48
and molecular rearrange-
ments,
49
were established to synthesize enantioenriched
allenes, efficient protocols toward this goal with a concise
manipulation are still highly sought after. Given that the
synthesis of racemic allenes are well established,
50,51
access to
optically active allenes through deracemization of racemic
allenes is a highly attractive but challenging strategy and
deserves to be investigated. The initial work by Weiss and co-
workers demonstrated that photochemical deracemization of
penta-2,3-diene with a chiral sensitizer through an energy
transfer pathway was feasible, but with very small enantiose-
lectivity (ca. 3.4% ee).
52
Extraordinary works by Bach and co-
workers elegantly showed that if a hydrogen bonding between
chiral sensitizer and the allenes was introduced, the efficiency
of the photocatalytic deracemization of allenes was improved
dramatically (up to 97% ee).
17
The different association
constants and sensitization efficiencies of hydrogen bonding
complexes between the chiral thioxanthone and each
enantiomer of the allene racemate ensure the observed
deracemization (Figure 1b).
Transition metal catalysis at its photoexcited states has
attracted significant attention for the discovery of unprece-
dented transformations.
53−56
In contrast to metallaphotoredox
catalysis, which employs photosensitizers and transition metals
synergistically,
57−61
photoexcited transition metal catalysis uses
a single transition metal complex to harvest light and enable
bond forming or breaking events. However, the double duty of
transition metal catalysis makes the asymmetric version of this
catalytic mode formidably challenging, and few enantioselec-
tive excited transition metal catalytic transformations were
reported.
62−69
Very recently, our group succeeded in achieving
the kinetic resolution of 2-styrylpyrrolidines enabled by
photoexcited chiral copper complex-mediated alkene E → Z
isomerization.
70
The different overall sensitization rates
between the chiral copper complex and the two enantiomers
of 2-styrylpyrrolidines led to excellent kinetic resolution
efficiency. This success inspires us to investigate photoexcited
transition metal-mediated deracemization of racemic allenes
(Figure 1c). Energy from visible light can compensate for the
entropy loss. The complexes of a transition metal, a chiral
ligand, and chiral allenes are diastereomeric and chemically
distinguishable, wherein the principle of microscopic reversi-
bility is not applicable. Here, we show that fine-tuning of
ligand−substrate interactions can precisely create thermody-
namic biases to encompass the rapid photochemical deracem-
ization of allene racemates. The transition metal binds to the
allene directly, and the preinstalled binding site can be avoided,
which can expand the scope of allenes significantly.

Reaction Investigation. Toward this end, we initiated the
investigation utilizing configurationally stable aryl-alkyl dis-
ubstituted allene rac-1 as a model substrate. After a quick
screening, it was regretfully found that the chiral copper
complex under visible light irradiation was an ineffective
catalytic system for the deracemization of allene rac-1. We had
to turn our attention to other transition metal-based
photocatalytic systems. Given that allenes can coordinate to
palladium, we focused on the development of photoexcited
palladium catalysis for the deracemization of allenes. This
adjustment turned out to be fruitful. After careful and thorough

Proposed Mechanism and DFT Calculations. Based on
the aforementioned kinetic and spectral data, a possible
principle for this photochemical deracemization was proposed.
As shown in Figure 3a, the coordination of Pd/L1 with R-
allene is favored due to ligand−substrate steric repulsions and
the thermodynamically favored Pd/L1/R-allene complex is
easier to be excited to undergo the metal-to-ligand charge
transfer process.
71−74
Thus, the R-allene can racemize rapidly,
while S-allene remains largely intact during the period of
reaction time, which is the decisive factor for excellent
deracemization efficiency.

Substrate Scope and Limitation. With the optimal
reaction conditions established, the generality and limitation of
this deracemization protocol were evaluated (Figure 4). The
cautious monitoring of the ee with time exhibited that the
photochemical deracemization of different substrates reached
photostationary states within 1.5−6 h under optimized
conditions. To our delight, various aryl-alkyl disubstituted
allenes were well-tolerated in this transformation and provided
highly enantioenriched allenes in 89−97% yields with 86−95%
ee. We first focused on the alkyl moieties. Substituents with
different electronic properties at different positions on the
phenyl rings of the alkyl chain had a negligible effect on the
enantioselectivity (S-1−12). Chain length of the alkyl group
and cyclic alkyl group (S-13−17) did not affect the
enantioselectivity either. The sterically hindered tert-butyl
group had no significant influence on this deracemization
transformation (95% yield and 88% ee for S-17) in terms of
yield and enantioselectivity, but with a longer reaction (6 h). A
broad range of functional groups on the skeleton of aliphatic
substituents, such as ester (S-18), amide (S-19), ether (S-20),
amine (S-21), hydroxy group (S-22), and silyl ether (S-23),
were all tolerated. To further expand the scope of the
photochemical deracemization, a range of allenes with diverse
substitution patterns on aryl moieties were then tested.
Similarly, no obvious substitution effect was found (S-24−
31). Heteroaromatic groups, such as furan (S-32), thiophene
(S-33), quinoline (S-34), and benzofuran (S-35), proved to be
competent reaction partners. Other structurally diverse allenes
(S-36, S-37, and S-38) could also be prepared with good yields
(91−92% yields) and enantioselectivities (80−94% ee). We
next turned our attention to aryl−aryl disubstituted allenes. We
were pleased to find that photochemical deracemization of
aryl−aryl disubstituted allenes was also efficient, giving the
desired chiral deracemized products (S-39−53) with excellent
enantiopurity (86−95% ee) and yields (85−96%). Substituents
with different electronic properties at different positions on the
aryl rings of aryl−aryl disubstituted allenes were well tolerated
in this reaction. Allenes containing thiophene and furan (S-44
and S-45) proved to be competent reaction partners.
Disappointedly, alkyl−alkyl disubstituted and trisubstituted
allenes tested so far were not effective under standard
conditions in terms of enantioselectivity (For more un-
successful substrates, see Figure S1 in the Supporting
Information). The absolute configuration of products was
established ambiguously by single-crystal X-ray diffraction
analysis of allene S-52.
77
Synthetic Practicality and Applications. To demon-
strate the synthetic utility of this protocol, a scale-up reaction
and some useful transformations were conducted (Figure 5).
The photochemical deracemization of rac-26 on a 4.0 mol
scale was applied under the optimal reaction conditions. This
scaled reaction worked smoothly, and the enantioenriched
product S-26 (1.04 g) was obtained in 4 h with a comparable
yield and enantioselectivity (90% yield and 91% ee). The TBS
group of deracemization product S-26 could be conveniently
removed with TBAF in THF to provide synthetically versatile
allenyl alcohol 54 without loss of any optical purity.
Subsequently, a series of transformations from allenyl alcohol
54 were performed. The allenyl alcohol 54 could be converted
to the corresponding allenyl bromide 55 under Appel’s
conditions (PPh
3
and CBr
4
) in an 83% yield without affecting
the optical purity (90% ee).
78
The enantioenriched allenyl
alcohols were identified as valuable intermediates in the
construction of chiral heterocycles. Treatment of the allenyl
alcohol 54 with AgNO

79

also accessed in the assistance of NIS in an 80% yield with

CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed an unprecedented photo-
excited palladium-catalyzed deracemization of disubstituted
allenes under mild reaction conditions. A series of structurally
diverse disubstituted allenes bearing primary alcohol, sensitive
secondary amine, ester, N-Boc, ether, etc. were suitable in the
established protocol with excellent yields and enantioselectiv-
ities. The resultant functionalized enantioenriched allenes can
be easily transformed to a series of synthetically useful
